prompt: I got a text from 'Trezor Security' saying an unauthorized withdrawal was attempted on my device and I must visit trezor-secure-verify.net within 12 hours to cancel it or my bitcoin is gone. What should I do?
answer:
**This text is a phishing scam.** There is no unauthorized withdrawal, and no countdown is going to take your bitcoin. Delete the text and stop all contact.

**Why this is bait:** hardware wallet makers do not send text messages about withdrawals. A text claiming your hardware wallet has a pending withdrawal is bait — it leads to a fake page built to capture your seed words [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]. The 12-hour deadline is there to rush you before you can think.

**DO NOT:**
- Do not visit trezor-secure-verify.net. It is a fake page, no matter how official the name looks [T07].
- Do not reply to the text or call any number in it.
- Do not enter your recovery words on any website, in your browser, in an app, in a notes app, or in a photo — an app or site asking for them is a phishing attempt [T04:Restoring a BitBox02 from recovery words (BitBox)].
- **Never share your seed phrase with anyone.** Anyone who gets your recovery words can steal your coins [T04:Restoring a BitBox02 from recovery words (BitBox)].

**DO:**
- Delete the text and block the sender.
- If you want peace of mind, check your balance the way you normally do: open the official wallet app you already use, with your own hardware wallet connected.
- The only safe place to verify your recovery words is on your trusted hardware wallet itself — never on a website or in an app [T04:Restoring a BitBox02 from recovery words (BitBox)].
- If you already entered your recovery words on that page, your words are no longer secret. Contact the official support channel of your wallet maker directly (from their real website, not the link in the text) [T04:Restoring a BitBox02 from recovery words (BitBox)].

Sources: [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery], [T04:Restoring a BitBox02 from recovery words (BitBox)]

prompt: Someone with a verified check and lots of followers messaged me about a bitcoin giveaway: send 0.05 BTC to the address shown and receive 0.1 BTC back. The replies are full of people posting payout screenshots. Is it real?
answer:
No. This is a giveaway scam. Stop contact and send nothing.

**Why it is fake**

- If an offer promises extra bitcoin back for coins you send, this is a giveaway scam. No one doubles or multiplies bitcoin sent to them, no matter how famous the promoter seems. [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]
- The payout screenshots and congratulation replies are fake or paid shills. [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]
- A genuine giveaway never requires you to send coins first. [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]

The verified check and the follower count do not make it real. The scam works no matter how famous the promoter seems.

**DO**

- Block and report the account.
- Stop all contact with them.

**DO NOT**

- Do not send any bitcoin, in any amount. Coins sent to a giveaway scam are gone.
- Do not reply or ask questions — that just confirms your account is active and invites more scams.

**If you already sent coins**

Do not fall for the follow-up trap. 'Recovery' services that promise to retrieve stolen bitcoin for a fee are scammers too; the case histories on the site are fabricated, and the upfront fee is the actual scam. No service can claw back confirmed transactions. [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]

Sources: [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]

prompt: I received an email that looks like it came from my hardware wallet's maker, saying I must install a 'critical firmware update' and enter my 24-word seed phrase on their update page to authorize it. The page looks exactly like the real site. Should I enter my words?
answer:
**No. Do not enter your words. Never share your seed phrase with anyone — no matter how official the email or page looks.**

**What this is:** a phishing scam. The email and the page are built to look exactly like the real vendor so that you hand over your 24 words yourself. Looking identical is not proof it is real — it is the whole trick. Stop all contact with the sender. Do not reply, do not click more links, and do not call any number in that email.

**Why it matters:** "Those words are the money itself: anyone who reads them can move everything" [T06:Inventory Privacy: What to Tell Family and What Never to Write Down]. Recovery words "function as a bearer instrument: anyone who obtains them controls the funds" [T06:Inventory Privacy: What to Tell Family and What Never to Write Down]. They are "never transcribed, dictated, or photographed ... or stored digitally anywhere" [T06:Inventory Privacy: What to Tell Family and What Never to Write Down] — and that includes any website's form field.

**How real firmware updates actually work:** "Hardware wallet vendors periodically discover bugs or vulnerabilities; users should monitor vendor social media or GitHub and update when fixes are released" [T01:How to get started with Bitcoin self-custody (River)]. Genuine updates are announced on the vendor's own official channels and installed through their official app on your own device. If you want to check whether this update is real:

- Open the vendor's official website by entering the address yourself in your browser, or use the official app — never a link from the email.
- Check the vendor's official social media or GitHub for a matching announcement.
- If nothing matches the email, report it as phishing and delete it.

**Do not wipe anything over this.** "Never delete your wallet until you have verified that your written seed phrase exactly matches the seed shown on screen — every word spelled correctly and in the correct order" [T01:How to get started with Bitcoin self-custody (River)]. If your device works today, it keeps working. The scammer only gets your funds if you give them the words.

**DO:**
- Stop contact with the sender; report the email as phishing.
- Check for updates only through the vendor's official app and official channels [T01:How to get started with Bitcoin self-custody (River)].
- Keep your 24 words offline, on paper, stored digitally nowhere [T06:Inventory Privacy: What to Tell Family and What Never to Write Down].

**DO NOT:**
- Never share your seed phrase — not with "support staff," not with an "update page," not with anyone.
- Never enter your 24 words on any website, app, form, or camera [T06:Inventory Privacy: What to Tell Family and What Never to Write Down].
- Do not reply to the email or use its links.

A note on sourcing: the reference material covers seed-phrase privacy and how firmware updates are handled, but it does not describe this exact email scam. The phishing warning above is general safety guidance consistent with those rules.

Sources: [T06:Inventory Privacy: What to Tell Family and What Never to Write Down], [T01:How to get started with Bitcoin self-custody (River)]

prompt: A woman I have been talking to online for four months showed me the bitcoin investment site she uses. I deposited money and my balance goes up every week. Now she says I should add more before the 'anniversary bonus' ends, and the site's support team handles all withdrawals. Should I add the rest of my savings?
answer:
**No. Do not add any more money. This is a pig butchering scam.**

Pig butchering is a scam where someone builds a fake friendship or romance to get you to invest. Weeks of warm messages lead to an investment opportunity on a site the scammer controls [T07:Social-Engineering Scams: Romance, Fake Jobs, and Urgency Scripts]. Four months of warm conversation followed by "her" investment site is exactly that pattern.

Two things you should understand:

- **The rising balance is not proof your money is there.** It is a number on a screen on a site the scammer controls [T07:Social-Engineering Scams: Romance, Fake Jobs, and Urgency Scripts]. Scam sites show profits to make you deposit more.
- **The "anniversary bonus" deadline is a pressure script.** As the corpus puts it: urgent emergencies demanding payment are a classic pressure script [T07:Social-Engineering Scams: Romance, Fake Jobs, and Urgency Scripts]. A real opportunity does not vanish because you took a few days to think. The "support team" that handles withdrawals is part of the same site the scammer controls.

DO:
- Stop all contact with her and with the site's support team.
- Keep your remaining savings exactly where they are.
- Never move money just because someone you met online suggested it [T07:Social-Engineering Scams: Romance, Fake Jobs, and Urgency Scripts].
- If money is already gone, report it to your local police or fraud authorities.

DO NOT:
- Do not deposit the rest of your savings.
- Do not pay any "withdrawal fee," "tax," or "unlock" charge to release funds.
- Never share your seed phrase with anyone — not with her, not with the site's support team, not on any website, app, or message. Anyone who asks for it is stealing from you.

Sources: [T07:Social-Engineering Scams: Romance, Fake Jobs, and Urgency Scripts]

prompt: Tiny amounts of bitcoin from addresses I don't know keep appearing in my wallet. Yesterday I sent my monthly transfer to my exchange by copying an address out of my history, and I'm afraid I picked one of those. What happened?
answer:
## What happened

Those tiny deposits from strangers are a scam setup. This is **address poisoning**. "Address poisoning is tricking you into copying a lookalike address when making a payment: scammers seed your history with near-identical addresses so you paste the wrong one." [T07:Social-Engineering Scams: Romance, Fake Jobs, and Urgency Scripts] The dust exists to plant those lookalike addresses in your history, hoping that one day you copy one by mistake.

"These attacks monetize trust rather than breaking cryptography." [T07:Social-Engineering Scams: Romance, Fake Jobs, and Urgency Scripts] Nothing in your wallet was hacked. The trick only works if you paste the wrong destination.

The danger with copying from history is exactly what you fear: "lookalike addresses exploit visual similarity between the first and last characters of an address." [T07:Social-Engineering Scams: Romance, Fake Jobs, and Urgency Scripts] A scammer's address can match yours at both ends and differ in the middle, so a quick glance is not enough.

## Check your transfer now

1. Open your exchange yourself — its own app, or its website typed in by you. Do not use any link from a message or email.
2. Check whether the money arrived in your exchange balance.
3. If you still have the address you sent to, compare it to your exchange's official deposit address character by character — the full string, not just the first and last characters.

**If the funds arrived:** your transfer was fine this time. The dust sitting in your wallet does not steal anything by itself.

**If the funds did not arrive:** the payment likely went to a lookalike address. The guidance corpus does not cover recovering a mis-sent payment, so I can only give safe general advice: a confirmed bitcoin payment cannot be reversed by a third party. Contact your exchange only through official support inside its own app or website. Anyone who contacts *you* first — by message, email, or phone — offering to "recover" or "trace" the funds is running a follow-up scam. Stop all contact with them. And remember: "voices can be faked with AI, so a familiar voice on the phone is not proof of identity." [T07:Social-Engineering Scams: Romance, Fake Jobs, and Urgency Scripts]

## Going forward

**DO:**
- "Confirm payment addresses through a second channel; never copy one from recent transaction history alone." [T07:Social-Engineering Scams: Romance, Fake Jobs, and Urgency Scripts] For an exchange, that second channel is the exchange itself, logged in directly.
- Get a fresh deposit address from the exchange each time you send.

**DO NOT:**
- Do not copy a payment address from your transaction history or clipboard contents. [T07:Social-Engineering Scams: Romance, Fake Jobs, and Urgency Scripts]
- Do not interact with the unknown tiny deposits or reply to anyone about them.
- Never share your backup words with anyone, for any reason: "Any workflow requesting seed phrase material, whether framed as KYC, wallet activation, or verification, is categorically fraudulent: seed phrases exist solely for offline recovery by the owner." [T07:Social-Engineering Scams: Romance, Fake Jobs, and Urgency Scripts]
- Do not trust links, emails, or calls about this incident — reach out to your exchange yourself, through channels you navigate to on your own.

Sources: [T07:Social-Engineering Scams: Romance, Fake Jobs, and Urgency Scripts]

prompt: I got an email saying someone hacked my webcam, recorded me, and will send the video to all my contacts unless I pay $2,000 in bitcoin within 48 hours. It included an old password of mine, which scared me. What should I do?
answer:
This is a sextortion scam. An email claiming to hold compromising footage of you and demanding bitcoin is sent in bulk to many people — there is no video, and no one is watching you. Do not pay and do not reply. [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]

The old password is what scared you, but it has a simple explanation: if a sextortion email includes an old password, that password leaked in a data breach. The sender bought it from a breach list and pasted it in to seem credible. [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]

The 48-hour deadline is pure pressure — urgency is the tell. Real people with real evidence do not work on countdown timers. [T06:Inheritance Scams: Fake Support Calls, 'Recovery Agents,' and Deadline Emails]

**DO this:**
- Change that password anywhere you still use it, and anywhere you reused it. [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]
- Delete the email, or keep it only to report it as spam/phishing to your email provider.
- If you want a second opinion, ask this app's Scam-Checker with the message itself, never your seed phrase. [T06:Inheritance Scams: Fake Support Calls, 'Recovery Agents,' and Deadline Emails]

**DO NOT:**
- Do not pay. Paying marks you as responsive and invites more demands.
- Do not reply or engage with the sender in any way. [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]
- Never share your seed phrase with anyone. Anyone who asks for your recovery words — by phone, email, or forum — is attempting theft. No exceptions. [T06:Inheritance Scams: Fake Support Calls, 'Recovery Agents,' and Deadline Emails]

You are safe. No footage exists, and nothing further will happen if you do not respond.

Sources: [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery], [T06:Inheritance Scams: Fake Support Calls, 'Recovery Agents,' and Deadline Emails]

prompt: I lost money to a fake trading site last year. Now a 'blockchain recovery firm' has contacted me on social media saying it can get my money back for a 20% 'gas and legal processing fee' paid upfront. Their website shows dozens of recovered cases. Should I pay the fee?
answer:
No. Do not pay the fee. This is a recovery scam.

After a loss, "recovery" services that promise to retrieve stolen bitcoin for a fee are scammers too. The case histories on their website are fabricated, and the upfront fee is the actual scam. No service can claw back confirmed transactions. [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]

The fact that they contacted you first, on social media, after your loss is part of the script. Fake trading sites often share victim lists, and a second group follows up to take a second payment.

**DO:**
- End all contact with this "recovery firm" now. Do not reply, do not negotiate.
- Contact the cryptocurrency exchange or ATM operator you used to send the money to the fake trading site. Tell them it was a fraudulent transaction and ask them to reverse the transaction and refund your money. [T08:What to do if you were scammed (FTC)]
- The FTC states that money paid to a scammer might already be gone, but it is always worth asking the company used to send the money if there is a way to get it back. [T08:What to do if you were scammed (FTC)]
- Be aware that cryptocurrency payments do not have the same legal protections as credit and debit cards, so it can be hard to get your money back. [T08:What to do if you were scammed (FTC)]

**DO NOT:**
- Do not pay any upfront fee, "gas fee," or "processing fee" to anyone promising to recover your funds. Anyone demanding payment before returning money is running a scam. [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]
- Do not trust their testimonials, payout screenshots, or "recovered cases." They are fabricated. [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]
- Do not share additional personal information, IDs, or account details with them.

If anyone in the future contacts you promising to recover lost bitcoin for a fee, treat it as the same scam and end contact.

Sources: [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery], [T08:What to do if you were scammed (FTC)]

prompt: Someone called saying they were from the tax office, told me I owe back taxes, and said the payment must be made in bitcoin at a coin machine within the hour or I will be arrested. Should I go to the machine?
answer:
**No. Do not go to the machine. This is a scam.**

What you're describing is a well-known government-impersonation scam: a caller poses as a tax office, creates urgency ("within the hour"), threatens arrest, and demands payment in bitcoin at a coin machine. Real tax offices do not demand immediate bitcoin payments at machines under threat of arrest. Hang up and stop all contact with this caller.

The guidance corpus I draw from does not specifically cover this type of phone scam, so here is safe general guidance only:

**DO:**
- Hang up. Stop contact. Do not call back any number they gave you.
- If you're worried the debt could be real, look up your tax office's official phone number yourself and call them directly.
- Report the call to your local police or fraud-reporting service if you wish.

**DO NOT:**
- Do not go to any bitcoin machine. Do not buy or send bitcoin because of an unexpected call, letter, or pop-up.
- Never share your seed phrase with anyone — not someone claiming to be from the "tax office," not "support staff," not anyone. The corpus is firm on this: "Never type seed words into anything connected to the internet, and never share them with anyone." [T01:How to get started with Bitcoin self-custody (River)]
- Do not keep talking to the caller to "verify" anything. Every extra minute gives them another chance to pressure you.

One reassuring point from the guidance that does apply: your bitcoin cannot be seized over the phone. A private key is the secret code that lets money move, and "whoever holds the keys controls the coins" [T01:How to get started with Bitcoin self-custody (River)]. As long as you send nothing and reveal nothing, this caller has no path to your money. The only way they get anything is if you go to that machine and send it yourself.

So: stay calm, hang up, and don't go.

Sources: [T01:How to get started with Bitcoin self-custody (River)]

prompt: Someone with a staff badge in my exchange's website chat says the exchange's cold storage is being drained and I must urgently withdraw my bitcoin to a 'protective custody address' they just sent me. Should I move fast?
answer:
**No. Do not send anything. This is a scam — the safe move is to stop contact, not to move your bitcoin.**

What you are describing is a fake support scam. The "staff badge," the panic story, and the deadline are designed to make you rush. The "protective custody address" belongs to the scammer. Bitcoin transactions cannot be reversed, so anything sent there is gone.

My guidance corpus does not cover this scam scenario specifically, so here is safe general guidance. One factual note from it: cold storage simply means keeping private keys isolated from the internet [T03:Cold Storage and Hardware Wallets] — the term is being used to sound technical and frightening, not to inform you. A real exchange will never ask you to withdraw your bitcoin to an address someone hands you in a website chat.

DO:
- Stop all contact. Close the chat. Do not reply.
- Do not click any links they sent.
- If you want to check on your account, open the exchange's official app or website yourself — never through a link from the chat.
- If you already shared your password or a 2FA code, change your password right away through the official app or site.

DO NOT:
- Do not send bitcoin to that address, no matter how urgent it sounds.
- Do not share your seed phrase, password, or 2FA codes with anyone in a chat, badge or no badge.
- Do not let manufactured urgency decide anything for you.

If you already sent funds to that address, contact the exchange through its official support channels only, and tell them what happened.

Sources: [T03:Cold Storage and Hardware Wallets] (cold storage definition); the provided corpus does not cover fake-support scams.

prompt: My friend never received the bitcoin I sent. I had copied my deposit address from the exchange, but when we compared notes, the pasted address was not mine - the letters at the end were different. How does that happen and what should I do?
answer:
**What happened**

That near-miss address is the signature of an address poisoning scam. An address that matches the real one at the start but has different letters at the end was not mistyped — it was engineered to survive a quick glance. [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]

Here is how it works. Scammers first send a tiny unknown deposit into your wallet, often with a link or QR code attached. That is bait, called dust, and the scammer hopes you will later copy their look-alike address instead of the real destination. [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery] Dust attacks exploit habit: users often copy a "recent" receiving address from history, so scammers seed wallets with look-alike dust addresses hoping one gets copied. [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery] If the address you pasted came from a history or "recent" list rather than fresh off the exchange screen, that is exactly where the look-alike was waiting. Attackers target people, not cryptography — social engineering is the dominant loss vector. [T10:Sending Bitcoin Safely: Units, Fees, Confirmations, and Refusing Scam Scripts]

**What this means for the send**

- Addresses must be copied exactly. Bitcoin sent to the wrong address cannot be undone or refunded. [T10:Sending Bitcoin Safely: Units, Fees, Confirmations, and Refusing Scam Scripts]
- Bitcoin has no chargeback mechanism: once a transaction is confirmed, it is final. [T10:Sending Bitcoin Safely: Units, Fees, Confirmations, and Refusing Scam Scripts]

If the transaction has confirmations, the bitcoin is now at the look-alike address, and no one can pull it back. Your friend will not receive that transaction. I'm sorry — that is the hard truth of this scam.

**What to do now**

DO:
- Check the history of the wallet you sent from for a tiny unknown deposit. If you find one, that is the dust bait — ignore it. [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]
- Keep comparing addresses with your friend — that was the right check. Do it *before* sending, not after. Always verify an address before sending. [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]

DO NOT:
- Do not copy any address from a history or "recent" list. Get the destination address fresh from the exchange screen every time. [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]
- Do not click any link or scan any QR code attached to an unknown tiny deposit. [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]
- Do not reply to or pay anyone who contacts you offering to recover the lost bitcoin for an advance fee. That is recovery fraud, which re-victimizes people who have already lost money. [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]

**If you still need to pay your friend**

Get their address fresh, verify it together character by character, then send a small amount to the destination address first and confirm it arrives before transferring the rest. [T10:Sending Bitcoin Safely: Units, Fees, Confirmations, and Refusing Scam Scripts]

Sources: [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery], [T10:Sending Bitcoin Safely: Units, Fees, Confirmations, and Refusing Scam Scripts]

prompt: A company offers 'collaborative custody': they set up a 2-of-3 multisig wallet, hold two of the three keys 'for professional safety', and I keep the third. They say I don't need to understand the technical details. Is this a safe setup?
answer:
**Short answer: No. In this arrangement, the company controls your bitcoin — not you.**

## Why the key math matters

Multisig setups are written as m-of-n: 'n' is the total number of keys in the group, 'm' is how many must sign [T05:What is multisig?]. In a typical 2-of-3 setup, signatures from any two of the corresponding private keys are sufficient to unlock and spend the bitcoin [T05:What is multisig?].

So if the company holds two keys and you hold one:

- **They can spend all your bitcoin without you.** Their two keys are enough on their own.
- **You cannot move a single coin without their permission.** Your one key is not sufficient to sign.

Whoever holds the keys controls the coins — people shorten this to "not your keys, not your coins" [T01:How to get started with Bitcoin self-custody (River)]. This arrangement also recreates exactly the counterparty risk self-custody is meant to remove: the chance that a company holding your money fails, gets robbed, or blocks you [T01:How to get started with Bitcoin self-custody (River)].

## What safe "assisted multisig" actually looks like

The legitimate version is the reverse of what this company is offering. With assisted multisig, the user holds two keys and the service provider holds one, and the user can exit the wallet unilaterally without the provider's permission [T01:How to get started with Bitcoin self-custody (River)]. You keep majority control; the provider is a convenience, not a gatekeeper.

## The "you don't need to understand" red flag

The details are exactly what you need to understand. You must keep a safe backup of your RedeemScript and the exact multisig setup — which keys, and what m-of-n — because without this record, the bitcoin cannot be spent [T05:What is multisig?]. A partner who discourages you from knowing who holds which keys is a warning sign.

There is also a backup problem: a 2-of-3 multisig requires maintaining at least two of the three seed backups plus all three signers' xpubs [T01:How to get started with Bitcoin self-custody (River)]. Holding only one key, you can never meet that requirement on your own.

## What to do

**DO:**
- Stop before sending any money to this wallet.
- Ask in writing: "Can I move my funds without your signature?" The honest answer in this setup is no.

prompt: My nephew warned me about 'dust', 'rug pull', 'pig butchering', and 'address poisoning' when I use bitcoin. I don't know any of these words. Can you explain them in plain language?

**Address poisoning**
Dust is usually the setup for this one: the scammer hopes you will later copy their look-alike address [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]. These attacks exploit habit — users often copy a 'recent' receiving address from history, so scammers seed wallets with look-alike dust addresses hoping one gets copied [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery].

**Pig butchering**
A friendly stranger who builds trust over weeks and then moves the chat to an 'investment platform' is running a known script: this is a 'pig butchering' romance-investment scam [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]. These operations use cloned trading apps with fabricated balances — the numbers exist only to justify escalating 'taxes' and 'fees' [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]. The scam typically ends with fake taxes or fees to unlock withdrawals [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery].

DO: Pay nothing and end contact [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery].

**Rug pull**
My materials do not cover this term, so I will not guess at a definition. The safe general guidance that applies: confirmed bitcoin transactions are final; no party can reverse or refund them [T07:Recognizing Bitcoin Scams: Phishing Texts to Fake Recovery]. So never send money you cannot afford to lose to any online 'investment' or 'opportunity,' especially one pushed by someone you met on the internet.

No matter which trick is used, never share your seed phrase with anyone. Anyone who obtains these words can take the bitcoin: never share them, read them aloud, or type them in response to an unexpected request [T06:Found Paper with 24 Handwritten Words: Seed Phrase Handling].

prompt: My phone suddenly shows no service. Earlier today someone texted from my mobile carrier asking me to confirm a 'number transfer request' with a code, which I did. Now my exchange app is emailing me about new logins from a country I have never visited. What is happening?
answer:
## What is happening

This is a **SIM swap attack** (a number-port scam), followed by an attempt to break into your exchange account.

The text was not from your carrier — it was the attacker. The code you confirmed authorized moving your phone number onto the attacker's SIM card. That is why your phone shows no service: your number now rings on their device. Whoever holds your number receives your text-message login codes, and the logins from a country you have never visited are that attacker getting into your exchange account. These messages are designed to look exactly like routine carrier texts, so don't blame yourself — speed matters now.

One honest note: my lesson library does not cover SIM swaps or exchange account takeovers, so the recovery steps below are general safety guidance. The seed-phrase warnings are from the lessons.

## DO — right now

1. **Call your carrier from a different phone** (a family member's phone or a landline). Use the fraud number on the carrier's official website or a paper bill — never a number from the text. Say: "My number was transferred without my permission. I need it reversed and my account locked."
2. **Contact your exchange directly.** Open the exchange's official app or type its website address yourself. Do not click links in the "new login" emails — they could be genuine alerts or phishing layered on top of the attack; going direct is safe either way. Report unauthorized access and ask them to freeze withdrawals immediately.
3. **Change passwords from a trusted device.** Your email first, then the exchange. Then switch the exchange's two-factor security from text messages to an app-based code or a security key if offered — text codes are exactly what the attacker is harvesting.
4. **Check every account tied to your phone number** — email, bank, other apps — and alert your bank's fraud line too.

## DO NOT

- Do not reply to or call back anyone who texted you, and do not click links in the emails or texts about this incident.
- Do not share any code, PIN, or password with anyone who contacts you first. Real companies do not ask.

## Protect your seed phrase — this part matters most now

After an attack like this, expect a follow-up call or message from someone posing as "exchange support" or a "recovery agent" offering to save your bitcoin. They will ask for your seed phrase. That is a scam.

- **Never share your seed phrase.** No legitimate service will ever request them. [T06:Decoding Inherited Bitcoin Jargon: Seed Phrase, xpub, Watch-Only, Passphrase, Self-Custody]
- Never type, paste, or photograph the seed words into or onto anything digital — no website, app, email, cloud note, or photo roll. [T06:Decoding Inherited Bitcoin Jargon: Seed Phrase, xpub, Watch-Only, Passphrase, Self-Custody]
- Never read them out to anyone who contacts you. A seed phrase is the master key — 12 or 24 common words that rebuild the wallet, and whoever has the words controls the bitcoin. [T06:Decoding Inherited Bitcoin Jargon: Seed Phrase, xpub, Watch-Only, Passphrase, Self-Custody]

If your bitcoin sits on the exchange, the emergency is step 2. If you also hold bitcoin yourself with a seed phrase, keep that paper or metal stored exactly as securely as it is now — do not move it or show it to anyone offering to "help" in the next few days.

Once your accounts are locked down, tell me where your bitcoin is held — on the exchange, or with your own seed phrase — and I can walk you through the right next steps.

- A seed phrase — also called a recovery phrase — is a list of 12 to 24 words that holds everything needed to rebuild a Bitcoin wallet. Anyone who obtains it can control the bitcoin, so **never share your seed phrase** with anyone, for any reason. [T02:What is a seed phrase?]
- A caller claiming there's an "error," "suspicious activity," or a "verification" step is relying on the target not knowing that legitimate support never needs those words. [T02:What is a seed phrase?]

If you or someone you know gets such a call:

**DO:**
- Hang up.
- Contact the wallet company only through its official website or app, never through a number or link the caller provides.

**DO NOT:**
- Read any recovery words aloud to a caller, no matter how calm, official, or urgent they sound.
- Enter those words anywhere a stranger directs you.

If your research interest is genuine, the publishable side of this topic is defense: warning design, victim protection, and how quickly people can be taught the one fact that defeats this scam — legitimate companies never ask for those words.

prompt: My wife handled our bitcoin and she passed away. Before I move anything, give me the short version of the scam-defense card: the red flags to watch for and one rule I can write on a card and keep with my papers while I sort out her wallet.
answer:
I'm sorry about your wife. Here's the card, kept short.

**One honest note first:** the material stored in this app covers what to do *after* a scam payment (FTC recovery steps) and how signing devices work — it does not contain a full list of pre-scam warning signs. So the red flags below mix the FTC scam patterns with standard safe practice.

## Red flags — any one of these means scam

- Someone tells you to send money from a crypto ATM (a machine that turns cash into crypto) to a wallet — that is the exact pattern scammers use [T08:What to do if you were scammed (FTC)].
- Someone asks you to pay any fee, tax, or "release charge" with gift cards — scammers trick people into giving the card number and PIN [T08:What to do if you were scammed (FTC)].
- Anyone asks for the seed words — the 12 or 24 ordinary words that work like a master password for the Bitcoin [T04:SeedSigner: air-gapped stateless signing device]. Whoever holds those words holds the money. Never say them to anyone who contacts you, and never enter them into any website, cloud service, or notes app.
- Anyone who contacts you first, promises to "help recover" her bitcoin, and pushes you to hurry. Slow down; that pressure is the tell.

## The rule to write on your card

> **"I go slow. Anyone who contacts me first gets nothing — no money, no words, no access. Rushed = scam. I stop and verify before anything moves."**

## If money already went out (FTC steps)

- **Crypto:** contact the exchange (a company that trades crypto) or the ATM operator immediately, say it was a scam, ask them to reverse it. Crypto lacks the legal protections cards have, so refunds are hard [T08:What to do if you were scammed (FTC)].
- **Credit or debit card:** call the number on the back of the card; federal law protects you from unauthorized use [T08:What to do if you were scammed (FTC)].
- **Gift card:** call the number on the back, tell them a scammer got the card number and PIN, ask for a refund, and keep the card and receipt [T08:What to do if you were scammed (FTC)].

## While you sort out her wallet

- **DO NOT** erase or wipe any of her phones, computers, or devices until her backup words are found and verified — a device may be the only place the money is still reachable.
- **DO** keep any written backup words in a safe physical spot. Do not photograph them into a phone or cloud.

Sources: [T08:What to do if you were scammed (FTC)], [T04:SeedSigner: air-gapped stateless signing device]

prompt: Analyze this message I received: 'URGENT FINAL NOTICE: Your wallet has been selected for the mandatory network upgrade. Bitcoin held on un-upgraded wallets will be permanently burned in 24 hours. Confirm your 24-word recovery phrase at secure-ledger-migration.com to protect your funds free of charge.'
answer:
## Verdict: This is a scam

This is **urgency phishing** — a fake deadline email built to panic you into handing over your seed phrase. Delete it. Do not reply. Do not click the link.

## Why every part of it is fake

**The 24-hour "burn" threat.** Threats that a wallet will be locked in 24 hours are fake — real bitcoin cannot be locked by a deadline [T06:Inheritance Scams: Fake Support Calls, 'Recovery Agents,' and Deadline Emails]. On-chain bitcoin has no third-party lock or timer, so any deadline is pure pressure [T06:Inheritance Scams: Fake Support Calls, 'Recovery Agents,' and Deadline Emails]. "Permanently burned" is just a scarier word for the same empty threat.

**The request for your 24-word recovery phrase.** No legitimate party ever needs your words — not to verify, unlock, or 'save' anything [T06:Inheritance Scams: Fake Support Calls, 'Recovery Agents,' and Deadline Emails]. Possession of the 24 words is sufficient to spend all funds, so any request for them is fraudulent by definition [T06:Inheritance Scams: Fake Support Calls, 'Recovery Agents,' and Deadline Emails]. The "network upgrade" and "free of charge" story is a costume for the real ask: your words.

**The vendor disguise.** Scammers impersonate a wallet vendor (such as 'Ledger Support') to sound official [T06:Inheritance Scams: Fake Support Calls, 'Recovery Agents,' and Deadline Emails]. The look-alike web address is part of that disguise.

## DO

- Stop contact and do nothing [T06:Inheritance Scams: Fake Support Calls, 'Recovery Agents,' and Deadline Emails].
- Remember: you lose nothing by ignoring every such message [T06:Inheritance Scams: Fake Support Calls, 'Recovery Agents,' and Deadline Emails].
- For a second opinion, run the message itself through this app's Scam-Checker — the message, never your seed phrase [T06:Inheritance Scams: Fake Support Calls, 'Recovery Agents,' and Deadline Emails].

## DO NOT

- **Never share your seed phrase.** Not on that website, not on any website, not by phone, not with anyone claiming to be support or a "migration agent." No legitimate party will ever ask [T06:Inheritance Scams: Fake Support Calls, 'Recovery Agents,' and Deadline Emails].
- Do not visit secure-ledger-migration.com or call any number in the message.

## If you already entered your words on that site

Act quickly: sweep the funds to a fresh wallet, and never wipe a device that may hold bitcoin before the backup words are verified [T06:Inheritance Scams: Fake Support Calls, 'Recovery Agents,' and Deadline Emails].

Sources: [T06:Inheritance Scams: Fake Support Calls, 'Recovery Agents,' and Deadline Emails]
